[trait with optimizations to efficiently accept any Rust string type, and several other efficient conveniences.](https://docs.rs/rustix/*/rustix/path/trait.Arg.html)

`Arg``rustix` is low-level and, and while the `net` API supports Winsock2 on
Windows, the rest of the APIs do not support Windows; for higher-level and more
portable APIs built on this functionality, see the [ cap-std](https://crates.io/crates/cap-std),

[,](https://crates.io/crates/memfd)

`memfd`[, and](https://crates.io/crates/timerfd)

`timerfd`[crates, for example.](https://crates.io/crates/io-streams)

`io-streams``rustix` currently has two backends available:

-
linux_raw, which uses raw Linux system calls and vDSO calls, and is supported on Linux on x86-64, x86, aarch64, riscv64gc, powerpc64le, arm (v5 onwards), mipsel, and mips64el, with stable, nightly, and 1.63 Rust. - By being implemented entirely in Rust, avoiding `libc`,`errno`, and pthread cancellation, and employing some specialized optimizations, most functions compile down to very efficient code, which can often be fully inlined into user code.
- Most functions in `linux_raw`preserve memory, I/O safety, and pointer provenance all the way down to the syscalls.

- By being implemented entirely in Rust, avoiding
-
libc, which uses the `libc``libc`libraries on Unix-family platforms, and`windows-sys`

The linux_raw backend is enabled by default on platforms which support it. To
enable the libc backend instead, either enable the "use-libc" cargo feature,
or set the `RUSTFLAGS` environment variable to `--cfg=rustix_use_libc` when
building.

## Cargo features

The modules [ rustix::io](https://docs.rs/rustix/*/rustix/io/index.html),

[, and](https://docs.rs/rustix/*/rustix/fd/index.html)

`rustix::fd`[are enabled by default. The rest of the API is conditional with cargo feature flags:](https://docs.rs/rustix/*/rustix/ffi/index.html)

`rustix::ffi`| Name | Description |
|---|---|
| `event` | —Polling and event operations.`rustix::event` |
| `fs` | —Filesystem operations.`rustix::fs` |
| `io_uring` | —Linux io_uring.`rustix::io_uring` |
| `mm` | —Memory map operations.`rustix::mm` |
| `mount` | —Linux mount API.`rustix::mount` |
| `net` | —Network-related operations.`rustix::net` |
| `param` | —Process parameters.`rustix::param` |
| `pipe` | —Pipe operations.`rustix::pipe` |
| `process` | —Process-associated operations.`rustix::process` |
| `procfs` | —Utilities for reading`rustix::procfs``/proc`on Linux. |
| `pty` | —Pseudoterminal operations.`rustix::pty` |
| `rand` | —Random-related operations.`rustix::rand` |
| `shm` | —POSIX shared memory.`rustix::shm` |
| `stdio` | —Stdio-related operations.`rustix::stdio` |
| `system` | —System-related operations.`rustix::system` |
| `termios` | —Terminal I/O stream operations.`rustix::termios` |
| `thread` | —Thread-associated operations.`rustix::thread` |
| `time` | —Time-related operations.`rustix::time` |
| `use-libc` | Enable the libc backend. |

## 64-bit Large File Support (LFS) and Year 2038 (y2038) support

`rustix` automatically uses 64-bit APIs when available, and avoids exposing
32-bit APIs that would have the year-2038 problem or fail to support large
files. For instance, `rustix::fstatvfs` calls `fstatvfs64`, and returns a
struct that's 64-bit even on 32-bit platforms.

## Similar crates

`rustix` is similar to [ nix](https://crates.io/crates/nix),

[,](https://crates.io/crates/simple_libc)

`simple_libc`[,](https://crates.io/crates/unix)

`unix`[,](https://crates.io/crates/nc)

`nc`[, and](https://crates.io/crates/uapi)

`uapi`[.](https://lib.rs/crates/rusl)

`rusl``rustix` is architected for [I/O safety](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/blob/master/text/3128-io-safety.md)with most APIs using

[and](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/os/fd/struct.OwnedFd.html)

`OwnedFd`[to manipulate file descriptors rather than](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/os/fd/trait.AsFd.html)

`AsFd``File` or
even `c_int`, and supporting multiple backends so that it can use direct
syscalls while still being usable on all platforms `libc` supports. Like `nix`,
`rustix` has an optimized and flexible filename argument mechanism that allows
users to use a variety of string types, including non-UTF-8 string types.[ relibc](https://gitlab.redox-os.org/redox-os/relibc) is a similar project which aims to be a full "libc", including
C-compatible interfaces and higher-level C/POSIX standard-library
functionality;

`rustix` just aims to provide safe and idiomatic Rust interfaces
to low-level syscalls. `relibc` also doesn't tend to support features not
supported on Redox, such as `*at` functions like `openat`, which are important
features for `rustix`.`rustix` has its own code for making direct syscalls, similar to the
[ syscall](https://crates.io/crates/syscall),

[, and](https://crates.io/crates/sc)

`sc`[crates, using the Rust](https://crates.io/crates/scall)

`scall``asm!` macro.
`rustix` can also use Linux's vDSO mechanism to optimize Linux `clock_gettime`
on all architectures, and all Linux system calls on x86. And `rustix`'s
syscalls report errors using an optimized `Errno` type.`rustix`'s `*at` functions are similar to the [ openat](https://crates.io/crates/openat) crate, but

`rustix`
provides them as free functions rather than associated functions of a `Dir`
type. `rustix`'s `CWD` constant exposes the special `AT_FDCWD` value in a safe
way, so users don't need to open `.` to get a current-directory handle.`rustix`'s `openat2` function is similar to the [ openat2](https://crates.io/crates/openat2) crate, but uses I/O
safety types rather than

`RawFd`. `rustix` does not provide dynamic feature
detection, so users must handle the [error themselves.](https://docs.rs/rustix/*/rustix/io/struct.Errno.html#associatedconstant.NOSYS)

`NOSYS``rustix`'s `termios` module is similar to the [ termios](https://crates.io/crates/termios) crate, but uses I/O
safety types rather than

`RawFd`, and the flags parameters to functions such as
`tcsetattr` are `enum`s rather than bare integers. And, rustix calls its
`tcgetattr` function `tcgetattr`, rather than `Termios::from_fd`.## Minimum Supported Rust Version (MSRV)

This crate currently works on the version of [Rust on Debian stable](https://packages.debian.org/stable/rust/rustc), which is
currently [Rust 1.63](https://blog.rust-lang.org/2022/08/11/Rust-1.63.0.html). This policy may change in the future, in minor version
releases, so users using a fixed version of Rust should pin to a specific
version of this crate.

## Minimum Linux Version

On Linux platforms, rustix requires at least Linux 3.2. This is at most the oldest Linux version supported by:

- [any current Rust target](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/rustc/platform-support.html), or
- [kernel.org](https://www.kernel.org/releases.html)at the time of rustix's- [MSRV](https://docs.rs#minimum-supported-rust-version-msrv)release. The specifics of this policy may change in the future, but we intend it to always reflect “very old” Linux versions.

## 64-bit Large File Support (LFS) and Year 2038 (y2038) support

`rustix` automatically uses 64-bit APIs when available, and avoids exposing
32-bit APIs that would have the year-2038 problem or fail to support large
files. For instance, `rustix::fstatvfs` calls `fstatvfs64`, and returns a
struct that's 64-bit even on 32-bit platforms.

## Similar crates

`rustix` is similar to [ nix](https://crates.io/crates/nix),

[,](https://crates.io/crates/simple_libc)

`simple_libc`[,](https://crates.io/crates/unix)

`unix`[,](https://crates.io/crates/nc)

`nc`[, and](https://crates.io/crates/uapi)

`uapi`[.](https://lib.rs/crates/rusl)

`rusl``rustix` is architected for [I/O safety](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/blob/master/text/3128-io-safety.md)with most APIs using

[and](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/os/fd/struct.OwnedFd.html)

`AsFd``File` or
even `c_int`, and supporting multiple backends so that it can use direct
syscalls while still being usable on all platforms `libc` supports. Like `nix`,

users to use a variety of string types, including non-UTF-8 string types.[ relibc](https://gitlab.redox-os.org/redox-os/relibc) is a similar project which aims to be a full "libc", including
C-compatible interfaces and higher-level C/POSIX standard-library
functionality;

`rustix` just aims to provide safe and idiomatic Rust interfaces
to low-level syscalls. `relibc` also doesn't tend to support features not
supported on Redox, such as `*at` functions like `openat`, which are important
features for `rustix`.`rustix` has its own code for making direct syscalls, similar to the

[, and](https://crates.io/crates/sc)

`sc`[crates, using the Rust](https://crates.io/crates/scall)

on all architectures, and all Linux system calls on x86. And `rustix`'s
syscalls report errors using an optimized `Errno` type.`rustix`'s `*at` functions are similar to the [ openat](https://crates.io/crates/openat) crate, but

`rustix`
provides them as free functions rather than associated functions of a `Dir`
type. `rustix`'s `CWD` constant exposes the special `AT_FDCWD` value in a safe
way, so users don't need to open `.` to get a current-directory handle.`rustix`'s `openat2` function is similar to the [ openat2](https://crates.io/crates/openat2) crate, but uses I/O
safety types rather than

`RawFd`. `rustix` does not provide dynamic feature
detection, so users must handle the [error themselves.](https://docs.rs/rustix/*/rustix/io/struct.Errno.html#associatedconstant.NOSYS)

`NOSYS``rustix`'s `termios` module is similar to the [ termios](https://crates.io/crates/termios) crate, but uses I/O
safety types rather than

`RawFd`, and the flags parameters to functions such as
`tcsetattr` are `enum`s rather than bare integers. And, rustix calls its
`tcgetattr` function `tcgetattr`, rather than `Termios::from_fd`.## Minimum Supported Rust Version (MSRV)

# rustix 0.38.22 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rustix/0.38.22

A Bytecode Alliance project

`rustix` provides efficient memory-safe and [I/O-safe](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/blob/master/text/3128-io-safety.md) wrappers to POSIX-like,
Unix-like, Linux, and Winsock2 syscall-like APIs, with configurable backends.
It uses Rust references, slices, and return values instead of raw pointers, and
[I/O safety types](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/os/fd/index.html#structs) instead of raw file descriptors, providing memory safety,
[I/O safety](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/blob/master/text/3128-io-safety.md), and [provenance](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/95228). It uses `Result`s for reporting errors,
[ bitflags](https://crates.io/crates/bitflags) instead of bare integer flags, an

[trait with optimizations to efficiently accept any Rust string type, and several other efficient conveniences.](https://docs.rs/rustix/*/rustix/path/trait.Arg.html)

`Arg``rustix` is low-level and, and while the `net` API supports Winsock2 on
Windows, the rest of the APIs do not support Windows; for higher-level and more
portable APIs built on this functionality, see the [ cap-std](https://crates.io/crates/cap-std),

[,](https://crates.io/crates/memfd)

`memfd`[, and](https://crates.io/crates/timerfd)

`timerfd`[crates, for example.](https://crates.io/crates/io-streams)

`io-streams``rustix` currently has two backends available:

-
linux_raw, which uses raw Linux system calls and vDSO calls, and is supported on Linux on x86-64, x86, aarch64, riscv64gc, powerpc64le, arm (v5 onwards), mipsel, and mips64el, with stable, nightly, and 1.63 Rust. - By being implemented entirely in Rust, avoiding `libc`,`errno`, and pthread cancellation, and employing some specialized optimizations, most functions compile down to very efficient code, which can often be fully inlined into user code.
- Most functions in `linux_raw`preserve memory, I/O safety, and pointer provenance all the way down to the syscalls.

- By being implemented entirely in Rust, avoiding
-
libc, which uses the `libc``libc`libraries on Unix-family platforms, and`windows-sys`

The linux_raw backend is enabled by default on platforms which support it. To
enable the libc backend instead, either enable the "use-libc" cargo feature,
or set the `RUSTFLAGS` environment variable to `--cfg=rustix_use_libc` when
building.

supported on Redox, such as `*at` functions like `openat`, which are important
features for `rustix`.`rustix` has its own code for making direct syscalls, similar to the
[ syscall](https://crates.io/crates/syscall),

[, and](https://crates.io/crates/sc)

`sc`[crates, using the Rust](https://crates.io/crates/scall)

`scall``asm!` macro.
`rustix` can also use Linux's vDSO mechanism to optimize Linux `clock_gettime`
on all architectures, and all Linux system calls on x86. And `rustix`'s
syscalls report errors using an optimized `Errno` type.`rustix`'s `*at` functions are similar to the [ openat](https://crates.io/crates/openat) crate, but

`rustix`
provides them as free functions rather than associated functions of a `Dir`
type. `rustix`'s `CWD` constant exposes the special `AT_FDCWD` value in a safe
way, so users don't need to open `.` to get a current-directory handle.`rustix`'s `openat2` function is similar to the [ openat2](https://crates.io/crates/openat2) crate, but uses I/O
safety types rather than

`RawFd`. `rustix` does not provide dynamic feature
detection, so users must handle the [error themselves.](https://docs.rs/rustix/*/rustix/io/struct.Errno.html#associatedconstant.NOSYS)

`NOSYS``rustix`'s `termios` module is similar to the [ termios](https://crates.io/crates/termios) crate, but uses I/O
safety types rather than

`RawFd`, and the flags parameters to functions such as
`tcsetattr` are `enum`s rather than bare integers. And, rustix calls its
`tcgetattr` function `tcgetattr`, rather than `Termios::from_fd`.## Minimum Supported Rust Version (MSRV)

This crate currently works on the version of [Rust on Debian stable](https://packages.debian.org/stable/rust/rustc), which is
currently Rust 1.63. This policy may change in the future, in minor version
releases, so users using a fixed version of Rust should pin to a specific

# rustix 0.38.19 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rustix/0.38.19

A Bytecode Alliance project

`rustix` provides efficient memory-safe and [I/O-safe](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/blob/master/text/3128-io-safety.md) wrappers to POSIX-like,
Unix-like, Linux, and Winsock2 syscall-like APIs, with configurable backends.
It uses Rust references, slices, and return values instead of raw pointers, and
[I/O safety types](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/os/fd/index.html#structs) instead of raw file descriptors, providing memory safety,
[I/O safety](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/blob/master/text/3128-io-safety.md), and [provenance](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/95228). It uses `Result`s for reporting errors,
[ bitflags](https://crates.io/crates/bitflags) instead of bare integer flags, an

[trait with optimizations to efficiently accept any Rust string type, and several other efficient conveniences.](https://docs.rs/rustix/*/rustix/path/trait.Arg.html)

`Arg``rustix` is low-level and, and while the `net` API supports Winsock2 on
Windows, the rest of the APIs do not support Windows; for higher-level and more
portable APIs built on this functionality, see the [ cap-std](https://crates.io/crates/cap-std),

[,](https://crates.io/crates/memfd)

`memfd`[, and](https://crates.io/crates/timerfd)

`timerfd`[crates, for example.](https://crates.io/crates/io-streams)

`io-streams``rustix` currently has two backends available:

-
linux_raw, which uses raw Linux system calls and vDSO calls, and is supported on Linux on x86-64, x86, aarch64, riscv64gc, powerpc64le, arm (v5 onwards), mipsel, and mips64el, with stable, nightly, and 1.63 Rust. - By being implemented entirely in Rust, avoiding `libc`,`errno`, and pthread cancellation, and employing some specialized optimizations, most functions compile down to very efficient code, which can often be fully inlined into user code.
- Most functions in `linux_raw`preserve memory, I/O safety, and pointer provenance all the way down to the syscalls.

- By being implemented entirely in Rust, avoiding
-
libc, which uses the `libc``libc`libraries on Unix-family platforms, and`windows-sys`

The linux_raw backend is enabled by default on platforms which support it. To
enable the libc backend instead, either enable the "use-libc" cargo feature,
or set the `RUSTFLAGS` environment variable to `--cfg=rustix_use_libc` when
building.

## Cargo features

The modules [ rustix::io](https://docs.rs/rustix/*/rustix/io/index.html),

[, and](https://docs.rs/rustix/*/rustix/fd/index.html)

`rustix::fd`[are enabled by default. The rest of the API is conditional with cargo feature flags:](https://docs.rs/rustix/*/rustix/ffi/index.html)

`rustix::ffi`| Name | Description |
|---|---|
| `event` | —Polling and event operations.`rustix::event` |
| `fs` | —Filesystem operations.`rustix::fs` |
| `io_uring` | —Linux io_uring.`rustix::io_uring` |
| `mm` | —Memory map operations.`rustix::mm` |
| `mount` | —Linux mount API.`rustix::mount` |
| `net` | —Network-related operations.`rustix::net` |
| `param` | —Process parameters.`rustix::param` |
| `pipe` | —Pipe operations.`rustix::pipe` |
| `process` | —Process-associated operations.`rustix::process` |
| `procfs` | —Utilities for reading`rustix::procfs``/proc`on Linux. |
| `pty` | —Pseudoterminal operations.`rustix::pty` |
| `rand` | —Random-related operations.`rustix::rand` |
| `shm` | —POSIX shared memory.`rustix::shm` |
| `stdio` | —Stdio-related operations.`rustix::stdio` |
| `system` | —System-related operations.`rustix::system` |
| `termios` | —Terminal I/O stream operations.`rustix::termios` |
| `thread` | —Thread-associated operations.`rustix::thread` |
| `time` | —Time-related operations.`rustix::time` |
| `use-libc` | Enable the libc backend. |

## 64-bit Large File Support (LFS) and Year 2038 (y2038) support

`rustix` automatically uses 64-bit APIs when available, and avoids exposing
32-bit APIs that would have the year-2038 problem or fail to support large
files. For instance, `rustix::fstatvfs` calls `fstatvfs64`, and returns a
struct that's 64-bit even on 32-bit platforms.

Windows, the rest of the APIs do not support Windows; for higher-level and more
portable APIs built on this functionality, see the [ cap-std](https://crates.io/crates/cap-std),

[,](https://crates.io/crates/memfd)

`memfd`[, and](https://crates.io/crates/timerfd)

`timerfd`[crates, for example.](https://crates.io/crates/io-streams)

`io-streams``rustix` currently has two backends available:

-
linux_raw, which uses raw Linux system calls and vDSO calls, and is supported on Linux on x86-64, x86, aarch64, riscv64gc, powerpc64le, arm (v5 onwards), mipsel, and mips64el, with stable, nightly, and 1.63 Rust. - By being implemented entirely in Rust, avoiding `libc`,`errno`, and pthread cancellation, and employing some specialized optimizations, most functions compile down to very efficient code, which can often be fully inlined into user code.
- Most functions in `linux_raw`preserve memory, I/O safety, and pointer provenance all the way down to the syscalls.

- By being implemented entirely in Rust, avoiding
-
libc, which uses the `libc``libc`libraries on Unix-family platforms, and`windows-sys`

The linux_raw backend is enabled by default on platforms which support it. To
enable the libc backend instead, either enable the "use-libc" cargo feature,
or set the `RUSTFLAGS` environment variable to `--cfg=rustix_use_libc` when
building.

## Cargo features

The modules [ rustix::io](https://docs.rs/rustix/*/rustix/io/index.html),

[, and](https://docs.rs/rustix/*/rustix/fd/index.html)

`rustix::fd`[are enabled by default. The rest of the API is conditional with cargo feature flags:](https://docs.rs/rustix/*/rustix/ffi/index.html)

`rustix::ffi`| Name | Description |
|---|---|
| `event` | —Polling and event operations.`rustix::event` |
| `fs` | —Filesystem operations.`rustix::fs` |
| `io_uring` | —Linux io_uring.`rustix::io_uring` |
| `mm` | —Memory map operations.`rustix::mm` |
| `mount` | —Linux mount API.`rustix::mount` |
| `net` | —Network-related operations.`rustix::net` |
| `param` | —Process parameters.`rustix::param` |
| `pipe` | —Pipe operations.`rustix::pipe` |
| `process` | —Process-associated operations.`rustix::process` |

| `pty` | —Pseudoterminal operations.`rustix::pty` |

| `shm` | —POSIX shared memory.`rustix::shm` |

| `system` | —System-related operations.`rustix::system` |

## 64-bit Large File Support (LFS) and Year 2038 (y2038) support

`rustix` automatically uses 64-bit APIs when available, and avoids exposing
32-bit APIs that would have the year-2038 problem or fail to support large
files. For instance, `rustix::fstatvfs` calls `fstatvfs64`, and returns a
struct that's 64-bit even on 32-bit platforms.

provides them as free functions rather than associated functions of a `Dir`

`RawFd`. `rustix` does not provide dynamic feature

`NOSYS``rustix`'s `termios` module is similar to the [ termios](https://crates.io/crates/termios) crate, but uses I/O
safety types rather than

`RawFd`, and the flags parameters to functions such as
`tcsetattr` are `enum`s rather than bare integers. And, rustix calls its
`tcgetattr` function `tcgetattr`, rather than `Termios::from_fd`.## Minimum Supported Rust Version (MSRV)

32-bit APIs that would have the year-2038 problem or fail to support large
files. For instance, `rustix::fstatvfs` calls `fstatvfs64`, and returns a
struct that's 64-bit even on 32-bit platforms.

# rustix 0.38.12 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rustix/0.38.12

A Bytecode Alliance project

`rustix` provides efficient memory-safe and [I/O-safe](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/blob/master/text/3128-io-safety.md) wrappers to POSIX-like,
Unix-like, Linux, and Winsock2 syscall-like APIs, with configurable backends.
It uses Rust references, slices, and return values instead of raw pointers, and
[I/O safety types](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/os/fd/index.html#structs) instead of raw file descriptors, providing memory safety,
[I/O safety](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/blob/master/text/3128-io-safety.md), and [provenance](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/95228). It uses `Result`s for reporting errors,
[ bitflags](https://crates.io/crates/bitflags) instead of bare integer flags, an

[trait with optimizations to efficiently accept any Rust string type, and several other efficient conveniences.](https://docs.rs/rustix/*/rustix/path/trait.Arg.html)

`Arg``rustix` is low-level and, and while the `net` API supports Winsock2 on
Windows, the rest of the APIs do not support Windows; for higher-level and more
portable APIs built on this functionality, see the [ cap-std](https://crates.io/crates/cap-std),

[,](https://crates.io/crates/memfd)

`memfd`[, and](https://crates.io/crates/timerfd)

`timerfd`[crates, for example.](https://crates.io/crates/io-streams)

`io-streams``rustix` currently has two backends available:

-
linux_raw, which uses raw Linux system calls and vDSO calls, and is supported on Linux on x86-64, x86, aarch64, riscv64gc, powerpc64le, arm (v5 onwards), mipsel, and mips64el, with stable, nightly, and 1.63 Rust. - By being implemented entirely in Rust, avoiding `libc`,`errno`, and pthread cancellation, and employing some specialized optimizations, most functions compile down to very efficient code, which can often be fully inlined into user code.
- Most functions in `linux_raw`preserve memory, I/O safety, and pointer provenance all the way down to the syscalls.

- By being implemented entirely in Rust, avoiding
-
libc, which uses the `libc``libc`libraries on Unix-family platforms, and`windows-sys`

The linux_raw backend is enabled by default on platforms which support it. To
enable the libc backend instead, either enable the "use-libc" cargo feature,
or set the `RUSTFLAGS` environment variable to `--cfg=rustix_use_libc` when
building.

# rustix 0.38.9 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rustix/0.38.9

A Bytecode Alliance project

`rustix` provides efficient memory-safe and [I/O-safe](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/blob/master/text/3128-io-safety.md) wrappers to POSIX-like,
Unix-like, Linux, and Winsock2 syscall-like APIs, with configurable backends.
It uses Rust references, slices, and return values instead of raw pointers, and
[I/O safety types](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/os/fd/index.html#structs) instead of raw file descriptors, providing memory safety,
[I/O safety](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/blob/master/text/3128-io-safety.md), and [provenance](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/95228). It uses `Result`s for reporting errors,
[ bitflags](https://crates.io/crates/bitflags) instead of bare integer flags, an

[trait with optimizations to efficiently accept any Rust string type, and several other efficient conveniences.](https://docs.rs/rustix/*/rustix/path/trait.Arg.html)

`Arg``rustix` is low-level and, and while the `net` API supports Winsock2 on
Windows, the rest of the APIs do not support Windows; for higher-level and more
portable APIs built on this functionality, see the [ cap-std](https://crates.io/crates/cap-std),

[,](https://crates.io/crates/memfd)

`memfd`[, and](https://crates.io/crates/timerfd)

`timerfd`[crates, for example.](https://crates.io/crates/io-streams)

`io-streams``rustix` currently has two backends available:

-
linux_raw, which uses raw Linux system calls and vDSO calls, and is supported on Linux on x86-64, x86, aarch64, riscv64gc, powerpc64le, arm (v5 onwards), mipsel, and mips64el, with stable, nightly, and 1.63 Rust. - By being implemented entirely in Rust, avoiding `libc`,`errno`, and pthread cancellation, and employing some specialized optimizations, most functions compile down to very efficient code, which can often be fully inlined into user code.
- Most functions in `linux_raw`preserve memory, I/O safety, and pointer provenance all the way down to the syscalls.

- By being implemented entirely in Rust, avoiding
-
libc, which uses the `libc``libc`libraries on Unix-family platforms, and`windows-sys`

The linux_raw backend is enabled by default on platforms which support it. To
enable the libc backend instead, either enable the "use-libc" cargo feature,
or set the `RUSTFLAGS` environment variable to `--cfg=rustix_use_libc` when
building.

## 64-bit Large File Support (LFS) and Year 2038 (y2038) support

`rustix` automatically uses 64-bit APIs when available, and avoids exposing
32-bit APIs that would have the year-2038 problem or fail to support large
files. For instance, `rustix::fstatvfs` calls `fstatvfs64`, and returns a
struct that's 64-bit even on 32-bit platforms.

| `mm` | —Memory map operations.`rustix::mm` |
| `mount` | —Linux mount API.`rustix::mount` |
| `net` | —Network-related operations.`rustix::net` |
| `param` | —Process parameters.`rustix::param` |
| `pipe` | —Pipe operations.`rustix::pipe` |
| `process` | —Process-associated operations.`rustix::process` |
| `procfs` | —Utilities for reading`rustix::procfs``/proc`on Linux. |
| `pty` | —Pseudoterminal operations.`rustix::pty` |
| `rand` | —Random-related operations.`rustix::rand` |
| `stdio` | —Stdio-related operations.`rustix::stdio` |
| `system` | —System-related operations.`rustix::system` |
| `termios` | —Terminal I/O stream operations.`rustix::termios` |
| `thread` | —Thread-associated operations.`rustix::thread` |
| `time` | —Time-related operations.`rustix::time` |
| `use-libc` | Enable the libc backend. |

## 64-bit Large File Support (LFS) and Year 2038 (y2038) support

`rustix` automatically uses 64-bit APIs when available, and avoids exposing
32-bit APIs that would have the year-2038 problem or fail to support large
files. For instance, `rustix::fstatvfs` calls `fstatvfs64`, and returns a
struct that's 64-bit even on 32-bit platforms.

`rustix` is similar to [ nix](https://crates.io/crates/nix),

`unix`[, and](https://crates.io/crates/nc)

# rustix 0.38.5 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rustix/0.38.5

A Bytecode Alliance project

`rustix` provides efficient memory-safe and [I/O-safe](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/blob/master/text/3128-io-safety.md) wrappers to POSIX-like,
Unix-like, Linux, and Winsock2 syscall-like APIs, with configurable backends.
It uses Rust references, slices, and return values instead of raw pointers, and
[I/O safety types](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/os/fd/index.html#structs) instead of raw file descriptors, providing memory safety,
[I/O safety](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/blob/master/text/3128-io-safety.md), and [provenance](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/95228). It uses `Result`s for reporting errors,
[ bitflags](https://crates.io/crates/bitflags) instead of bare integer flags, an

[trait with optimizations to efficiently accept any Rust string type, and several other efficient conveniences.](https://docs.rs/rustix/*/rustix/path/trait.Arg.html)

`Arg``rustix` is low-level and, and while the `net` API supports Winsock2 on
Windows, the rest of the APIs do not support Windows; for higher-level and more
portable APIs built on this functionality, see the [ cap-std](https://crates.io/crates/cap-std),

[,](https://crates.io/crates/memfd)

`memfd`[, and](https://crates.io/crates/timerfd)

`timerfd`[crates, for example.](https://crates.io/crates/io-streams)

`io-streams``rustix` currently has two backends available:

-
linux_raw, which uses raw Linux system calls and vDSO calls, and is supported on Linux on x86-64, x86, aarch64, riscv64gc, powerpc64le, arm (v5 onwards), mipsel, and mips64el, with stable, nightly, and 1.63 Rust. - By being implemented entirely in Rust, avoiding `libc`,`errno`, and pthread cancellation, and employing some specialized optimizations, most functions compile down to very efficient code, which can often be fully inlined into user code.
- Most functions in `linux_raw`preserve memory, I/O safety, and pointer provenance all the way down to the syscalls.

- By being implemented entirely in Rust, avoiding
-
libc, which uses the `libc``libc`libraries on Unix-family platforms, and`windows-sys`

The linux_raw backend is enabled by default on platforms which support it. To
enable the libc backend instead, either enable the "use-libc" cargo feature,
or set the `RUSTFLAGS` environment variable to `--cfg=rustix_use_libc` when
building.

`rustix`'s syscalls report errors using an optimized `Errno` type.`rustix`'s `*at` functions are similar to the [ openat](https://crates.io/crates/openat) crate, but

`rustix`
provides them as free functions rather than associated functions of a `Dir`
type. `rustix`'s `CWD` constant exposes the special `AT_FDCWD` value in a safe
way, so users don't need to open `.` to get a current-directory handle.`rustix`'s `openat2` function is similar to the [ openat2](https://crates.io/crates/openat2) crate, but uses I/O
safety types rather than

`RawFd`. `rustix` does not provide dynamic feature
detection, so users must handle the [error themselves.](https://docs.rs/rustix/*/rustix/io/struct.Errno.html#associatedconstant.NOSYS)

`NOSYS``rustix`'s `termios` module is similar to the [ termios](https://crates.io/crates/termios) crate, but uses I/O
safety types rather than

`RawFd`, and the flags parameters to functions such as
`tcsetattr` are `enum`s rather than bare integers. And, rustix calls its
`tcgetattr` function `tcgetattr`, rather than `Termios::from_fd`.## Minimum Supported Rust Version (MSRV)

# rustix 0.38.2 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rustix/0.38.2

A Bytecode Alliance project

`rustix` provides efficient memory-safe and [I/O-safe](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/blob/master/text/3128-io-safety.md) wrappers to POSIX-like,
Unix-like, Linux, and Winsock2 syscall-like APIs, with configurable backends.
It uses Rust references, slices, and return values instead of raw pointers, and
[I/O safety types](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/os/fd/index.html#structs) instead of raw file descriptors, providing memory safety,
[I/O safety](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/blob/master/text/3128-io-safety.md), and [provenance](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/95228). It uses `Result`s for reporting errors,
[ bitflags](https://crates.io/crates/bitflags) instead of bare integer flags, an

[trait with optimizations to efficiently accept any Rust string type, and several other efficient conveniences.](https://docs.rs/rustix/*/rustix/path/trait.Arg.html)

`Arg``rustix` is low-level and, and while the `net` API supports Winsock2 on
Windows, the rest of the APIs do not support Windows; for higher-level and more
portable APIs built on this functionality, see the [ cap-std](https://crates.io/crates/cap-std),

[,](https://crates.io/crates/memfd)

`memfd`[, and](https://crates.io/crates/timerfd)

`timerfd`[crates, for example.](https://crates.io/crates/io-streams)

`io-streams``rustix` currently has two backends available:

-
linux_raw, which uses raw Linux system calls and vDSO calls, and is supported on Linux on x86-64, x86, aarch64, riscv64gc, powerpc64le, arm (v5 onwards), mipsel, and mips64el, with stable, nightly, and 1.63 Rust. - By being implemented entirely in Rust, avoiding `libc`,`errno`, and pthread cancellation, and employing some specialized optimizations, most functions compile down to very efficient code, which can often be fully inlined into user code.
- Most functions in `linux_raw`preserve memory, I/O safety, and pointer provenance all the way down to the syscalls.

- By being implemented entirely in Rust, avoiding
-
libc, which uses the `libc``libc`libraries on Unix-family platforms, and`windows-sys`

The linux_raw backend is enabled by default on platforms which support it. To
enable the libc backend instead, either enable the "use-libc" cargo feature,
or set the `RUSTFLAGS` environment variable to `--cfg=rustix_use_libc` when
building.

## Cargo features

The modules [ rustix::io](https://docs.rs/rustix/*/rustix/io/index.html),

[, and](https://docs.rs/rustix/*/rustix/fd/index.html)

`rustix::fd`[are enabled by default. The rest of the API is conditional with cargo feature flags:](https://docs.rs/rustix/*/rustix/ffi/index.html)

`rustix::ffi`| Name | Description |
|---|---|
| `event` | —Polling and event operations.`rustix::event` |
| `fs` | and`rustix::fs`—Filesystem operations.`rustix::path` |
| `io_uring` | —Linux io_uring.`rustix::io_uring` |
| `mm` | —Memory map operations.`rustix::mm` |
| `net` | and`rustix::net`—Network-related operations.`rustix::path` |
| `param` | —Process parameters.`rustix::param` |
| `pipe` | —Pipe operations.`rustix::pipe` |
| `process` | —Process-associated operations.`rustix::process` |
| `procfs` | —Utilities for reading`rustix::procfs``/proc`on Linux. |
| `pty` | —Pseudoterminal operations.`rustix::pty` |
| `rand` | —Random-related operations.`rustix::rand` |
| `stdio` | —Stdio-related operations.`rustix::stdio` |
| `system` | —System-related operations.`rustix::system` |
| `termios` | —Terminal I/O stream operations.`rustix::termios` |
| `thread` | —Thread-associated operations.`rustix::thread` |
| `time` | —Time-related operations.`rustix::time` |
| `use-libc` | Enable the libc backend. |

## 64-bit Large File Support (LFS) and Year 2038 (y2038) support

`rustix` automatically uses 64-bit APIs when available, and avoids exposing
32-bit APIs that would have the year-2038 problem or fail to support large
files. For instance, `rustix::fstatvfs` calls `fstatvfs64`, and returns a
struct that's 64-bit even on 32-bit platforms.

linux_raw, which uses raw Linux system calls and vDSO calls, and is supported on Linux on x86-64, x86, aarch64, riscv64gc, powerpc64le, arm (v5 onwards), mipsel, and mips64el, with stable, nightly, and 1.63 Rust. - By being implemented entirely in Rust, avoiding `libc`,`errno`, and pthread cancellation, and employing some specialized optimizations, most functions compile down to very efficient code, which can often be fully inlined into user code.
- Most functions in `linux_raw`preserve memory, I/O safety, and pointer provenance all the way down to the syscalls.

- By being implemented entirely in Rust, avoiding
-
libc, which uses the `libc``libc`libraries on Unix-family platforms, and`windows-sys`

The linux_raw backend is enabled by default on platforms which support it. To
enable the libc backend instead, either enable the "use-libc" cargo feature,
or set the `RUSTFLAGS` environment variable to `--cfg=rustix_use_libc` when
building.

## 64-bit Large File Support (LFS) and Year 2038 (y2038) support

`rustix` automatically uses 64-bit APIs when available, and avoids exposing
32-bit APIs that would have the year-2038 problem or fail to support large
files. For instance, `rustix::fstatvfs` calls `fstatvfs64`, and returns a
struct that's 64-bit even on 32-bit platforms.

`unix`[,](https://crates.io/crates/nc)

`nc`[, and](https://crates.io/crates/uapi)

`uapi`[.](https://lib.rs/crates/rusl)

`rusl``rustix` is architected for [I/O safety](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/blob/master/text/3128-io-safety.md)with most APIs using

[and](https://docs.rs/io-lifetimes/*/io_lifetimes/struct.OwnedFd.html)

`OwnedFd`[to manipulate file descriptors rather than](https://docs.rs/io-lifetimes/*/io_lifetimes/trait.AsFd.html)

`AsFd``File` or
even `c_int`, and supporting multiple backends so that it can use direct
syscalls while still being usable on all platforms `libc` supports. Like `nix`,
`rustix` has an optimized and flexible filename argument mechanism that allows
users to use a variety of string types, including non-UTF-8 string types.[ relibc](https://github.com/redox-os/relibc) is a similar project which aims to be a full "libc", including
C-compatible interfaces and higher-level C/POSIX standard-library
functionality;

`rustix` just aims to provide safe and idiomatic Rust interfaces
to low-level syscalls. `relibc` also doesn't tend to support features not
supported on Redox, such as `*at` functions like `openat`, which are important
features for `rustix`.`rustix` has its own code for making direct syscalls, similar to the [ sc](https://crates.io/crates/sc) and

[crates, though](https://crates.io/crates/scall)

`scall``rustix` can use either the Rust `asm!` macro or
out-of-line `.s` files so it supports Rust versions from 1.48 through Nightly.
`rustix` can also use Linux's vDSO mechanism to optimize Linux `clock_gettime`
on all architectures, and all Linux system calls on x86. And `rustix`'s
syscalls report errors using an optimized `Errno` type.`rustix`'s `*at` functions are similar to the [ openat](https://crates.io/crates/openat) crate, but

`rustix`
provides them as free functions rather than associated functions of a `Dir`
type. `rustix`'s `cwd()` function exposes the special `AT_FDCWD` value in a safe
way, so users don't need to open `.` to get a current-directory handle.`rustix`'s `openat2` function is similar to the [ openat2](https://crates.io/crates/openat2) crate, but uses I/O
safety types rather than

`RawFd`. `rustix` does not provide dynamic feature
detection, so users must handle the [error themselves.](https://docs.rs/rustix/*/rustix/io/struct.Errno.html#associatedconstant.NOSYS)

`NOSYS``rustix`'s `termios` module is similar to the [ termios](https://crates.io/crates/termios) crate, but uses I/O
safety types rather than

`RawFd`, and the flags parameters to functions such as
`tcsetattr` are `enum`s rather than bare integers. And, rustix calls its
`tcgetattr` function `tcgetattr`, rather than `Termios::from_fd`.## Minimum Supported Rust Version (MSRV)

This crate currently works on the version of [Rust on Debian stable](https://packages.debian.org/stable/rust/rustc), which is
currently Rust 1.48. This policy may change in the future, in minor version
releases, so users using a fixed version of Rust should pin to a specific
version of this crate.

# rustix 0.37.27 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rustix/0.37.27

A Bytecode Alliance project

`rustix` provides efficient memory-safe and [I/O-safe](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/blob/master/text/3128-io-safety.md) wrappers to POSIX-like,
Unix-like, Linux, and Winsock2 syscall-like APIs, with configurable backends.
It uses Rust references, slices, and return values instead of raw pointers, and
[ io-lifetimes](https://crates.io/crates/io-lifetimes) instead of raw file descriptors, providing memory safety,

[I/O safety](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/blob/master/text/3128-io-safety.md), and

[provenance](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/95228). It uses

`Result`s for reporting errors,
[instead of bare integer flags, an](https://crates.io/crates/bitflags)

`bitflags`[trait with optimizations to efficiently accept any Rust string type, and several other efficient conveniences.](https://docs.rs/rustix/*/rustix/path/trait.Arg.html)

`Arg``rustix` is low-level and, and while the `net` API supports Winsock2 on
Windows, the rest of the APIs do not support Windows; for higher-level and more
portable APIs built on this functionality, see the [ cap-std](https://crates.io/crates/cap-std),

[,](https://crates.io/crates/memfd)

`memfd`[, and](https://crates.io/crates/timerfd)

`timerfd`[crates, for example.](https://crates.io/crates/io-streams)

`io-streams``rustix` currently has two backends available:

-
linux_raw, which uses raw Linux system calls and vDSO calls, and is supported on Linux on x86-64, x86, aarch64, riscv64gc, powerpc64le, arm (v5 onwards), mipsel, and mips64el, with stable, nightly, and 1.48 Rust. - By being implemented entirely in Rust, avoiding `libc`,`errno`, and pthread cancellation, and employing some specialized optimizations, most functions compile down to very efficient code, which can often be fully inlined into user code.
- Most functions in `linux_raw`preserve memory, I/O safety, and pointer provenance all the way down to the syscalls.

- By being implemented entirely in Rust, avoiding
-
libc, which uses the `libc``libc`libraries on Unix-family platforms, and`windows-sys`

The linux_raw backend is enabled by default on platforms which support it. To
enable the libc backend instead, either enable the "use-libc" cargo feature,
or set the `RUSTFLAGS` environment variable to `--cfg=rustix_use_libc` when
building.

## Cargo features

The modules [ rustix::io](https://docs.rs/rustix/*/rustix/io/index.html),

[, and](https://docs.rs/rustix/*/rustix/fd/index.html)

`rustix::fd`[are enabled by default. The rest of the API is conditional with cargo feature flags:](https://docs.rs/rustix/*/rustix/ffi/index.html)

`rustix::ffi`| Name | Description |
|---|---|
| `fs` | and`rustix::fs`—Filesystem operations.`rustix::path` |
| `io_uring` | —Linux io_uring.`rustix::io_uring` |
| `mm` | —Memory map operations.`rustix::mm` |
| `net` | and`rustix::net`—Network-related operations.`rustix::path` |
| `param` | —Process parameters.`rustix::param` |
| `process` | —Process-associated operations.`rustix::process` |
| `pty` | —Pseduoterminal operations.`rustix::pty` |
| `rand` | —Random-related operations.`rustix::rand` |
| `termios` | —Terminal I/O stream operations.`rustix::termios` |
| `thread` | —Thread-associated operations.`rustix::thread` |
| `time` | —Time-related operations.`rustix::time` |
| `use-libc` | Enable the libc backend. |

## 64-bit Large File Support (LFS) and Year 2038 (y2038) support

`rustix` automatically uses 64-bit APIs when available, and avoids exposing
32-bit APIs that would have the year-2038 problem or fail to support large
files. For instance, `rustix::fstatvfs` calls `fstatvfs64`, and returns a
struct that's 64-bit even on 32-bit platforms.

Windows, the rest of the APIs do not support Windows; for higher-level and more
portable APIs built on this functionality, see the [ cap-std](https://crates.io/crates/cap-std),

[,](https://crates.io/crates/memfd)

`memfd`[, and](https://crates.io/crates/timerfd)

`timerfd`[crates, for example.](https://crates.io/crates/io-streams)

`io-streams``rustix` currently has two backends available:

-
linux_raw, which uses raw Linux system calls and vDSO calls, and is supported on Linux on x86-64, x86, aarch64, riscv64gc, powerpc64le, arm (v5 onwards), mipsel, and mips64el, with stable, nightly, and 1.48 Rust. - By being implemented entirely in Rust, avoiding `libc`,`errno`, and pthread cancellation, and employing some specialized optimizations, most functions compile down to very efficient code, which can often be fully inlined into user code.
- Most functions in `linux_raw`preserve memory, I/O safety, and pointer provenance all the way down to the syscalls.

- By being implemented entirely in Rust, avoiding
-
libc, which uses the `libc``libc`libraries on Unix-family platforms, and`windows-sys`

The linux_raw backend is enabled by default on platforms which support it. To
enable the libc backend instead, either enable the "use-libc" cargo feature,
or set the `RUSTFLAGS` environment variable to `--cfg=rustix_use_libc` when
building.

## Cargo features

The modules [ rustix::io](https://docs.rs/rustix/*/rustix/io/index.html),

[, and](https://docs.rs/rustix/*/rustix/fd/index.html)

`rustix::fd`[are enabled by default. The rest of the API is conditional with cargo feature flags:](https://docs.rs/rustix/*/rustix/ffi/index.html)

`rustix::ffi`| Name | Description |
|---|---|
| `fs` | and`rustix::fs`—Filesystem operations.`rustix::path` |
| `io_uring` | —Linux io_uring.`rustix::io_uring` |
| `mm` | —Memory map operations.`rustix::mm` |
| `net` | and`rustix::net`—Network-related operations.`rustix::path` |
| `param` | —Process parameters.`rustix::param` |
| `process` | —Process-associated operations.`rustix::process` |
| `pty` | —Pseduoterminal operations.`rustix::pty` |
| `rand` | —Random-related operations.`rustix::rand` |
| `termios` | —Terminal I/O stream operations.`rustix::termios` |
| `thread` | —Thread-associated operations.`rustix::thread` |
| `time` | —Time-related operations.`rustix::time` |
| `use-libc` | Enable the libc backend. |

## 64-bit Large File Support (LFS) and Year 2038 (y2038) support

`rustix` automatically uses 64-bit APIs when available, and avoids exposing
32-bit APIs that would have the year-2038 problem or fail to support large
files. For instance, `rustix::fstatvfs` calls `fstatvfs64`, and returns a
struct that's 64-bit even on 32-bit platforms.

## Similar crates

`rustix` is similar to [ nix](https://crates.io/crates/nix),

[,](https://crates.io/crates/simple_libc)

`simple_libc`[,](https://crates.io/crates/unix)

`unix`[,](https://crates.io/crates/nc)

`nc`[, and](https://crates.io/crates/uapi)

`uapi`[.](https://lib.rs/crates/rusl)

`rusl``rustix` is architected for [I/O safety](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/blob/master/text/3128-io-safety.md)with most APIs using

[and](https://docs.rs/io-lifetimes/*/io_lifetimes/struct.OwnedFd.html)

`OwnedFd`[to manipulate file descriptors rather than](https://docs.rs/io-lifetimes/*/io_lifetimes/trait.AsFd.html)

`AsFd``File` or
even `c_int`, and supporting multiple backends so that it can use direct
syscalls while still being usable on all platforms `libc` supports. Like `nix`,
`rustix` has an optimized and flexible filename argument mechanism that allows
users to use a variety of string types, including non-UTF-8 string types.[ relibc](https://github.com/redox-os/relibc) is a similar project which aims to be a full "libc", including
C-compatible interfaces and higher-level C/POSIX standard-library
functionality;

`rustix` just aims to provide safe and idiomatic Rust interfaces
to low-level syscalls. `relibc` also doesn't tend to support features not
supported on Redox, such as `*at` functions like `openat`, which are important
features for `rustix`.`rustix` has its own code for making direct syscalls, similar to the [ sc](https://crates.io/crates/sc) and

[crates, though](https://crates.io/crates/scall)

`scall``rustix` can use either the Rust `asm!` macro or
out-of-line `.s` files so it supports Rust versions from 1.48 through Nightly.
`rustix` can also use Linux's vDSO mechanism to optimize Linux `clock_gettime`
on all architectures, and all Linux system calls on x86. And `rustix`'s
syscalls report errors using an optimized `Errno` type.`rustix`'s `*at` functions are similar to the [ openat](https://crates.io/crates/openat) crate, but

`rustix`
provides them as free functions rather than associated functions of a `Dir`
type. `rustix`'s `cwd()` function exposes the special `AT_FDCWD` value in a safe
way, so users don't need to open `.` to get a current-directory handle.`rustix`'s `openat2` function is similar to the [ openat2](https://crates.io/crates/openat2) crate, but uses I/O
safety types rather than

`RawFd`. `rustix` does not provide dynamic feature
detection, so users must handle the [error themselves.](https://docs.rs/rustix/*/rustix/io/struct.Errno.html#associatedconstant.NOSYS)

`NOSYS``rustix`'s `termios` module is similar to the [ termios](https://crates.io/crates/termios) crate, but uses I/O
safety types rather than

`RawFd`, and the flags parameters to functions such as
`tcsetattr` are `enum`s rather than bare integers. And, rustix calls its
`tcgetattr` function `tcgetattr`, rather than `Termios::from_fd`.## Minimum Supported Rust Version (MSRV)

This crate currently works on the version of [Rust on Debian stable](https://packages.debian.org/stable/rust/rustc), which is
currently Rust 1.48. This policy may change in the future, in minor version
releases, so users using a fixed version of Rust should pin to a specific
version of this crate.

features for `rustix`.`rustix` has its own code for making direct syscalls, similar to the [ sc](https://crates.io/crates/sc) and

[crates, though](https://crates.io/crates/scall)

`scall``rustix` can use either the Rust `asm!` macro or
out-of-line `.s` files so it supports Rust versions from 1.48 through Nightly.
`rustix` can also use Linux's vDSO mechanism to optimize Linux `clock_gettime`
on all architectures, and all Linux system calls on x86. And `rustix`'s
syscalls report errors using an optimized `Errno` type.`rustix`'s `*at` functions are similar to the [ openat](https://crates.io/crates/openat) crate, but

`rustix`
provides them as free functions rather than associated functions of a `Dir`
type. `rustix`'s `cwd()` function exposes the special `AT_FDCWD` value in a safe
way, so users don't need to open `.` to get a current-directory handle.`rustix`'s `openat2` function is similar to the [ openat2](https://crates.io/crates/openat2) crate, but uses I/O
safety types rather than

`RawFd`. `rustix` does not provide dynamic feature
detection, so users must handle the [error themselves.](https://docs.rs/rustix/*/rustix/io/struct.Errno.html#associatedconstant.NOSYS)

`NOSYS``rustix`'s `termios` module is similar to the [ termios](https://crates.io/crates/termios) crate, but uses I/O
safety types rather than

`RawFd`, and the flags parameters to functions such as
`tcsetattr` are `enum`s rather than bare integers. And, rustix calls its
`tcgetattr` function `tcgetattr`, rather than `Termios::from_fd`.## Minimum Supported Rust Version (MSRV)

This crate currently works on the version of [Rust on Debian stable](https://packages.debian.org/stable/rust/rustc), which is
currently Rust 1.48. This policy may change in the future, in minor version
releases, so users using a fixed version of Rust should pin to a specific
version of this crate.

# rustix 0.37.20 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rustix/0.37.20

A Bytecode Alliance project

`rustix` provides efficient memory-safe and [I/O-safe](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/blob/master/text/3128-io-safety.md) wrappers to POSIX-like,
Unix-like, Linux, and Winsock2 syscall-like APIs, with configurable backends.
It uses Rust references, slices, and return values instead of raw pointers, and
[ io-lifetimes](https://crates.io/crates/io-lifetimes) instead of raw file descriptors, providing memory safety,

[I/O safety](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/blob/master/text/3128-io-safety.md), and

[provenance](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/95228). It uses

`Result`s for reporting errors,
[instead of bare integer flags, an](https://crates.io/crates/bitflags)

`bitflags`[trait with optimizations to efficiently accept any Rust string type, and several other efficient conveniences.](https://docs.rs/rustix/*/rustix/path/trait.Arg.html)

`Arg``rustix` is low-level and, and while the `net` API supports Winsock2 on
Windows, the rest of the APIs do not support Windows; for higher-level and more
portable APIs built on this functionality, see the [ cap-std](https://crates.io/crates/cap-std),

[,](https://crates.io/crates/memfd)

`memfd`[, and](https://crates.io/crates/timerfd)

`timerfd`[crates, for example.](https://crates.io/crates/io-streams)

`io-streams``rustix` currently has two backends available:

-
linux_raw, which uses raw Linux system calls and vDSO calls, and is supported on Linux on x86-64, x86, aarch64, riscv64gc, powerpc64le, arm (v5 onwards), mipsel, and mips64el, with stable, nightly, and 1.48 Rust. - By being implemented entirely in Rust, avoiding `libc`,`errno`, and pthread cancellation, and employing some specialized optimizations, most functions compile down to very efficient code, which can often be fully inlined into user code.
- Most functions in `linux_raw`preserve memory, I/O safety, and pointer provenance all the way down to the syscalls.

- By being implemented entirely in Rust, avoiding
-
libc, which uses the `libc``libc`libraries on Unix-family platforms, and`windows-sys`

The linux_raw backend is enabled by default on platforms which support it. To
enable the libc backend instead, either enable the "use-libc" cargo feature,
or set the `RUSTFLAGS` environment variable to `--cfg=rustix_use_libc` when
building.

## Cargo features

The modules [ rustix::io](https://docs.rs/rustix/*/rustix/io/index.html),

[, and](https://docs.rs/rustix/*/rustix/fd/index.html)

`rustix::fd`[are enabled by default. The rest of the API is conditional with cargo feature flags:](https://docs.rs/rustix/*/rustix/ffi/index.html)

`rustix::ffi`| Name | Description |
|---|---|
| `fs` | and`rustix::fs`—Filesystem operations.`rustix::path` |
| `io_uring` | —Linux io_uring.`rustix::io_uring` |
| `mm` | —Memory map operations.`rustix::mm` |
| `net` | and`rustix::net`—Network-related operations.`rustix::path` |
| `param` | —Process parameters.`rustix::param` |
| `process` | —Process-associated operations.`rustix::process` |
| `pty` | —Pseduoterminal operations.`rustix::pty` |
| `rand` | —Random-related operations.`rustix::rand` |
| `termios` | —Terminal I/O stream operations.`rustix::termios` |
| `thread` | —Thread-associated operations.`rustix::thread` |
| `time` | —Time-related operations.`rustix::time` |
| `use-libc` | Enable the libc backend. |

## 64-bit Large File Support (LFS) and Year 2038 (y2038) support

`rustix` automatically uses 64-bit APIs when available, and avoids exposing
32-bit APIs that would have the year-2038 problem or fail to support large
files. For instance, `rustix::fstatvfs` calls `fstatvfs64`, and returns a
struct that's 64-bit even on 32-bit platforms.

`rustix::ffi`| Name | Description |
|---|---|
| `fs` | and`rustix::fs`—Filesystem operations.`rustix::path` |
| `io_uring` | —Linux io_uring.`rustix::io_uring` |
| `mm` | —Memory map operations.`rustix::mm` |
| `net` | and`rustix::net`—Network-related operations.`rustix::path` |
| `param` | —Process parameters.`rustix::param` |
| `process` | —Process-associated operations.`rustix::process` |
| `rand` | —Random-related operations.`rustix::rand` |
| `termios` | —Terminal I/O stream operations.`rustix::termios` |
| `thread` | —Thread-associated operations.`rustix::thread` |
| `time` | —Time-related operations.`rustix::time` |
| `use-libc` | Enable the libc backend. |

## 64-bit Large File Support (LFS) and Year 2038 (y2038) support

`rustix` automatically uses 64-bit APIs when available, and avoids exposing
32-bit APIs that would have the year-2038 problem or fail to support large
files. For instance, `rustix::fstatvfs` calls `fstatvfs64`, and returns a
struct that's 64-bit even on 32-bit platforms.

## Similar crates

`rustix` is similar to [ nix](https://crates.io/crates/nix),

[,](https://crates.io/crates/simple_libc)

`simple_libc`[,](https://crates.io/crates/unix)

`unix`[, and](https://crates.io/crates/nc)

`nc`[.](https://crates.io/crates/uapi)

`uapi``rustix` is architected for [I/O safety](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/blob/master/text/3128-io-safety.md)with most APIs using

[and](https://docs.rs/io-lifetimes/*/io_lifetimes/struct.OwnedFd.html)

`OwnedFd`[to manipulate file descriptors rather than](https://docs.rs/io-lifetimes/*/io_lifetimes/trait.AsFd.html)

`AsFd``File` or
even `c_int`, and supporting multiple backends so that it can use direct
syscalls while still being usable on all platforms `libc` supports. Like `nix`,
`rustix` has an optimized and flexible filename argument mechanism that allows
users to use a variety of string types, including non-UTF-8 string types.[ relibc](https://github.com/redox-os/relibc) is a similar project which aims to be a full "libc", including
C-compatible interfaces and higher-level C/POSIX standard-library
functionality;

`rustix` just aims to provide safe and idiomatic Rust interfaces
to low-level syscalls. `relibc` also doesn't tend to support features not
supported on Redox, such as `*at` functions like `openat`, which are important
features for `rustix`.`rustix` has its own code for making direct syscalls, similar to the [ sc](https://crates.io/crates/sc) and

[crates, though](https://crates.io/crates/scall)

`scall``rustix` can use either the Rust `asm!` macro or
out-of-line `.s` files so it supports Rust versions from 1.48 through Nightly.
`rustix` can also use Linux's vDSO mechanism to optimize Linux `clock_gettime`
on all architectures, and all Linux system calls on x86. And `rustix`'s
syscalls report errors using an optimized `Errno` type.`rustix`'s `*at` functions are similar to the [ openat](https://crates.io/crates/openat) crate, but

`rustix`
provides them as free functions rather than associated functions of a `Dir`
type. `rustix`'s `cwd()` function exposes the special `AT_FDCWD` value in a safe
way, so users don't need to open `.` to get a current-directory handle.`rustix`'s `openat2` function is similar to the [ openat2](https://crates.io/crates/openat2) crate, but uses I/O
safety types rather than

`RawFd`. `rustix` does not provide dynamic feature
detection, so users must handle the [error themselves.](https://docs.rs/rustix/*/rustix/io/struct.Errno.html#associatedconstant.NOSYS)

`NOSYS``rustix`'s `termios` module is similar to the [ termios](https://crates.io/crates/termios) crate, but uses I/O
safety types rather than

`RawFd`, and the flags parameters to functions such as
`tcsetattr` are `enum`s rather than bare integers. And, rustix calls its
`tcgetattr` function `tcgetattr`, rather than `Termios::from_fd`.## Minimum Supported Rust Version (MSRV)

This crate currently works on the version of [Rust on Debian stable](https://packages.debian.org/stable/rust/rustc), which is
currently Rust 1.48. This policy may change in the future, in minor version
releases, so users using a fixed version of Rust should pin to a specific
version of this crate.

# rustix 0.37.16 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rustix/0.37.16

A Bytecode Alliance project

`rustix` provides efficient memory-safe and [I/O-safe](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/blob/master/text/3128-io-safety.md) wrappers to POSIX-like,
Unix-like, Linux, and Winsock2 syscall-like APIs, with configurable backends.
It uses Rust references, slices, and return values instead of raw pointers, and
[ io-lifetimes](https://crates.io/crates/io-lifetimes) instead of raw file descriptors, providing memory safety,

[I/O safety](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/blob/master/text/3128-io-safety.md), and

[provenance](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/95228). It uses

`Result`s for reporting errors,
[instead of bare integer flags, an](https://crates.io/crates/bitflags)

`bitflags`[trait with optimizations to efficiently accept any Rust string type, and several other efficient conveniences.](https://docs.rs/rustix/*/rustix/path/trait.Arg.html)

`Arg``rustix` is low-level and, and while the `net` API supports Winsock2 on
Windows, the rest of the APIs do not support Windows; for higher-level and more
portable APIs built on this functionality, see the [ cap-std](https://crates.io/crates/cap-std),

[,](https://crates.io/crates/memfd)

`memfd`[, and](https://crates.io/crates/timerfd)

`timerfd`[crates, for example.](https://crates.io/crates/io-streams)

`io-streams``rustix` currently has two backends available:

-
linux_raw, which uses raw Linux system calls and vDSO calls, and is supported on Linux on x86-64, x86, aarch64, riscv64gc, powerpc64le, arm (v5 onwards), mipsel, and mips64el, with stable, nightly, and 1.48 Rust. - By being implemented entirely in Rust, avoiding `libc`,`errno`, and pthread cancellation, and employing some specialized optimizations, most functions compile down to very efficient code, which can often be fully inlined into user code.
- Most functions in `linux_raw`preserve memory, I/O safety, and pointer provenance all the way down to the syscalls.

- By being implemented entirely in Rust, avoiding
-
libc, which uses the `libc``libc`libraries on Unix-family platforms, and`windows-sys`

The linux_raw backend is enabled by default on platforms which support it. To
enable the libc backend instead, either enable the "use-libc" cargo feature,
or set the `RUSTFLAGS` environment variable to `--cfg=rustix_use_libc` when
building.
